title: LCA in a BST
description: In a BST, walk down from root: if both p, q < root go left, both > root go right, else root IS the split point and therefore the LCA.

notes: BST ordering is the whole trick — you never need to search both subtrees like in a generic binary tree.
The first node where p and q diverge (one goes left, other right) OR equals one of them IS the LCA.
Iterative form is O(1) space; the recursive version is O(h) for the call stack.

questions.q: Why does the BST version beat the generic tree LCA?
options: BST ordering lets you pick ONE subtree at each step instead of searching both
Generic LCA does not work on BSTs

questions.q: When both p.val and q.val are greater than node.val, you go:

options: Both descendants are on the same side
p and q split (one goes left, one right) OR node equals p or q
O(h) where h is tree height

exercises.prompt: Fill in the iterative BST LCA. Tighten by going LEFT when both targets are smaller, RIGHT when both are larger.

blanks.hint: both targets smaller than the current node

L3.prompt: Write `lowestCommonAncestor(root, p, q)` for a BST. Build [6,2,8,0,4,7,9,null,null,3,5] and log the LCA of (2,8), (2,4), and (3,5) — each `.val` on its own line.
hints: Use the BST ordering — never recurse into both subtrees.
Loop while node is not null; split point (or hitting p/q) is the answer.
LCA(2,4) is 2 itself because 2 is an ancestor of 4.
